texts: mixed: nothing is lost -- day 210, Year 1 and past tense all sit straight on the equinox itself -- but 'came' is an arrival verb, and the rule that lets a date attach directly to an event noun names only occurred / happened / took place, so the translator had to stretch it. One word settles it: 'On day 210 of Year 1, the spring equinox occurred.' Separately, 'day 210' lands in the ordinary day-of-month slot, which carries no day-of-year reading -- a corpus-wide calendar gap no rewrite can close.
good. the moon gets its full state as its own referent plus the plain 'the moon was full' fact, with day 216 and Year 1 both carried.

bad: 'at the full-moon meeting' was filed as a place, but a meeting is an occasion, not a location -- so the parse says the closing happened at a spot that is really another event. Use the word our translator reserves for nesting one event inside another: 'The Council closed the salt-bloom season during the full-moon meeting.'
good. the name, the production it resumed (marked as usual and as the Northcove's own) and the resume event with its tense are all there.

bad: 'during the following two weeks' went in as the length of the stepping-down itself -- claiming the step-down ran exactly two weeks -- and the anaphoric 'following', i.e. its ordering after the meeting, was dropped altogether; a forward window has no covered form at all (only backward ones, 'over the past six months', do). Split it into the two shapes that are covered, an explicit ordering plus a stated duration: 'After the full-moon meeting, the stations of the Cliff Path stepped down salt-bloom additions for two weeks.'

bad: 'returned to spring levels' put the end point in the slot for a physical destination, which the scalar-change rules forbid outright -- an end value given as a word rather than a figure with a unit has no covered form, so the endpoint is either mis-filed (as here) or lost. Re-say it as an ordinary predication about the levels: 'The thread harvests matched their spring levels again.' If you have a figure, the measured form ('rose to forty bundles a week') is covered as well.

mixed: everything but the comparison lands -- Cauldron Hall, the distillation cycle, the beginning, the tense -- but 'heavier' is dropped, because a comparative with nothing stated to compare against has no covered form and our instructions say to drop it rather than assert plain 'heavy'. Name what it is heavier than and it is carried: 'Cauldron Hall began a distillation cycle heavier than the winter cycle.'

good. the three weeks of supply, the holding and the end-of-the-winter timing all land. Both 'three weeks of supply' and 'at the end of the winter' are constructions the instruction set does not cover head-on, but the parse improvises them without asserting anything false, so no rewrite is needed.

bad: 'about ten' has no covered form -- an exact count needs a plain whole number, and the vague-count phrases ('several', 'dozens') only cover wordings with no number in them -- so the hedge was pushed into the count slot as a spread, which is the wrong kind of value there. 'By the spring equinox' has no deadline form either when the deadline is an event rather than a date, so it came out as strictly before the equinox. Give a plain count and an explicit ordering: 'Before the spring equinox, ten sky-cats were visible on the cliff-spires in the morning.' If the number really is approximate, a bound works too -- 'at least eight sky-cats'.
